(1) Data preprocessing
Before using machine learning algorithms, log data needs to be preprocessed. The steps include
data cleaning (removing irrelevant data, correcting erroneous data), normalization (unifying
log formats), feature extraction (extracting meaningful information from logs as input to the
model), etc. Effective data preprocessing can greatly improve the efficiency of model training
and prediction accuracy.
(2) Feature engineering
Feature engineering is a vital part of machine learning, involving the selection, modification, and
creation of new features to enhance model performance. In log analysis, common features include
the timestamp of log entries, source IP addresses, error codes, operation codes, etc. Advanced
features include keywords or phrases extracted from log text or statistical information based on
the event frequency within a time window.
(3) Selecting appropriate machine learning models
Selecting suitable machine learning models according to the characteristics of the log data and
business needs is essential. For anomaly detection, commonly used algorithms include clustering
algorithms, distance-based anomaly detection, and neural networks.
Typical clustering algorithms include K-means and DBSCAN. These unsupervised learning
algorithms can help identify natural groups in the data, with outliers usually not belonging to
any main group. In distance-based anomaly detection, typical examples are the Isolation Forest
algorithm and the LOF (Local Outlier Factor) algorithm, which identify anomalies by considering
the distance between data points and their neighbors. Among neural networks, autoencoders are
a typical example, mainly suitable for handling large-scale data sets and complex data structures.
They can learn the normal patterns of data and identify anomalous data that deviate from these
patterns.
In 2024, at the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, a paper by Yunzhihui titled LOGFORMER: A
Pre-train and Tuning Pipeline for Log Anomaly Detection elaborated on how to use machine learning
techniques for log anomaly detection. According to the paper, Yunzhihui based their approach on
the Transformer model and used adapter fine-tuning to solve the semantic information sharing
issue between different log sources. Log anomaly detection is a key component in the field of
intelligent O&M. In real industrial scenarios, logs from different sources can vary significantly.
Early anomaly detection models only focused on extracting semantics from the log sequences of
the same source, resulting in poor generalization to logs from multiple different sources. Retraining
detection models with data from unknown log sources is inefficient.

Creating an audit policy
A policy file is used to control what events are recorded and where to store the logs, which can be a
standard log file or a webhook. We have included an example audit policy in the chapter7 directory
of the GitHub repository, and we will apply it to the KinD cluster that we have been using throughout
the book.
An audit policy is a collection of rules that tell the API server which API calls to log and how. When
Kubernetes parses the policy file, all rules are applied in order and only the initial matching policy event
will be applied. If you have more than one rule for a certain event, you may not receive the expected
data in your log files. For this reason, you need to be careful that your events are created correctly.
Policies use the audit.k8s.io API and the manifest kind of Policy. The following example shows
the beginning of a policy file:
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
rules:
- level: Request
userGroups: ["system:nodes"]
verbs: ["update","patch"]
resources:
- group: "" # core
resources: ["nodes/status", "pods/status"]
omitStages:
- "RequestReceived"
While a policy file may look like a standard Kubernetes manifest, you do not apply it using kubectl. A
policy file is used with the --audit-policy-file API flag on the API server(s). This will be explained
in the Enabling auditing on a cluster section.
To understand the rule and what it will log, we will go through each section in detail.
The first section of the rule is level, which determines the type of information that will be logged for
the event. There are four levels that can be assigned to events:
Table 7.1: Kubernetes auditing levels

The userGroups, verbs, and resources values tell the API server the object and action that will trigger
the auditing event. In this example, only requests from system:nodes that attempt an action of update
or patch on a node/status or pod/status on the core API will create an event.
omitStages tells the API server to skip any logging events during a stage, which helps you limit the
amount of data that is logged. There are four stages that an API request goes through:
Table 7.2: Auditing stages
In our example, we have set the event to ignore the RequestReceived event, which tells the API server
not to log any data for the incoming API request.

Understanding the LogFormer workflow
LogFormer addresses the above issues in two working phases: the Log Attention Encoding Phase
and the Cross-domain Adapter Fine-tuning Phase.
Preserving log semantics with Log Attention
The Log Attention Encoding Phase preserves semantic knowledge shared between different
domains. Specifically, to avoid information loss caused by log pattern parsing, the Log Attention
module models log sequences and makes additional use of parameter information that is neglected
in log pattern parsing, thereby achieving better performance. Compared to traditional structures,
the model additionally incorporates parameter information lost during log pattern parsing. The

SSH agent
If we decide to create an SSH key with a password to protect it (good choice), we will need to input
the password each time we want to use the key. So, in the end, it might be as insecure as having
to type in the password, as someone might be checking over our shoulder. To overcome this, we
can use a program called ssh-agent, which temporarily keeps the password in memory. This is
convenient and reduces the chances of someone watching while you type in your key.
When you’re using a graphical desktop, such as GNOME, as provided by SLES 16, the agent might
already be set up to start at session login. If you’re using a console (local or remote), the agent
must be started manually by executing ssh-agent.

so that we can make use of it, as shown in the following screenshot:
